newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy court grants house arrest to ex-Nazi Priebke.
newsitem.headline: Italy court grants house arrest to ex-Nazi Priebke.

text.p: An Italian military court on Tuesday granted house arrest to former SS captain Erich Priebke pending a re-trial for his role in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity, military prosecutor Antonino Intelisano said.
Intelisano, who has led the case against the 83-year-old German, announced the decision after the court met behind closed doors in Rome.
It ruled in favour of a request from defence lawyer Carlo Taormina to free his client from prison detention on grounds of deteriorating mental health.
Medical reports pointed to a loss of mental powers because of isolation and Priebke's advancing age, Taormina said.
Priebke has been remanded in jail, most recently in Rome's Forte Boccea military prison, since his extradition to Italy in November 1995 from Argentina, where he had lived openly since 1948.
It was not immediately clear when or where he would be moved. Judicial sources have said Priebke would probably be given shelter in a Roman Catholic convent or monastery.
Priebke is accused of complicity in multiple murder for his role in the SS massacre of 335 men and boys at the Ardeatine Caves near Rome on March 24, 1944. Seventy-five victims were Jews.
There was no immediate reaction to the court's decision from relatives of the victims.
Priebke has admitted taking part in the 1944 killings but has argued that he had to follow orders or would have been shot.

He has already been tried once for the crime by an Italian military court. Its verdict that he was guilty but should be allowed to go free caused outrage and was quashed in October on appeal. The re-trial is expected to start next month.

Another ex-Nazi, former SS major Karl Hass, is also accused of complicity in the massacre and judicial sources say the two men could be tried together. Hass, who is under house arrest in Rome, is due to go on trial on April 14.
A military court in Naples also met earlier on Tuesday to consider whether the arrest warrant issued after Priebke's first trial, which ended in uproar last August, was still valid.
It ruled that the detention order should not be revoked.
Priebke was re-arrested in the courtroom where his first trial took place on the night of the verdict after a siege by relatives of the massacre victims and other protesters.
